prompt: By the lesson, what is a diagram in relation to an architecture?
hint: A selection, by somebody, at some date, for some reader.

choices.text: The architecture itself, in its official form
choices.why: The architecture is what the running system does; the drawing is one person's selection of it.

choices.text: A view of it
choices.why: Right: one view, chosen for a question and a reader, which can agree with the system or not.

choices.text: A plan the code is required to follow
choices.why: That is the prescriptive architecture, and the slide shows how far a system drifts from a plan.

choices.text: Decoration for onboarding decks
choices.why: Diagrams are tools for thinking and explaining; the lesson keeps them, with four questions on their face.

prompt: Renata checks the 2021 slide by reading deployment manifests, database credentials, broker consumers and traces. Why those sources rather than interviews?
hint: What happens to the system when one of them is wrong?

choices.text: Engineers would not tell her the truth
choices.why: Nobody is accused of lying; people remember the plan, which is exactly what the slide shows.

choices.text: They are quicker to read than people are to schedule
choices.why: Speed is a side benefit; the argument is about which sources can drift.

choices.text: They cannot drift: the system breaks when they are wrong
choices.why: Right: a wrong credential stops a service, so these records describe what is, not what was intended.

choices.text: Architecture is defined as the deployment configuration
choices.why: Configuration is evidence of the structure, alongside traces and imports; it is not the definition.

prompt: Payments reads the monolith's loads table although the 2021 plan said each service would own its data. In Taylor, Medvidović and Dashofy's terms, what is that?
hint: Does it add to the plan, or contradict it?

choices.text: Drift
choices.why: Drift adds decisions the plan did not include without breaking it; this one breaks the ownership rule.

choices.text: Erosion
choices.why: Right: a decision that violates the intended architecture.

choices.text: Prescriptive architecture
choices.why: The prescriptive architecture is the intended one, the plan the read contradicts.

choices.text: A view mismatch
choices.why: The slide does mismatch the system, but the term for the code violating the plan is erosion.

prompt: Put the life of Carreto's slide in order, from when it was made to what Renata did with it.
hint: Intention first, replacement last.
items: It is drawn in 2021 as the plan for leaving the monolith
Payments connects to the loads table during an incident
Renata compares it with manifests, credentials and traces
She replaces it with dated evidence and a rough drawing

prompt: A team's wiki has no architecture diagram at all. Another team's wiki has a detailed one that is three years out of date. By the lesson, which is in the worse position, and why?
hint: Which one makes people ask questions?

choices.text: The first, because a missing diagram means a missing architecture
choices.why: Every system has an architecture drawn or not; the absence only leaves it undescribed.

choices.text: The second: a stale document that is believed
choices.why: Right: a missing diagram makes people ask, and a wrong one answers confidently with the wrong answer.

choices.text: Neither: diagrams do not affect how incidents are handled
choices.why: Carreto's slide sent engineers looking everywhere except the shared database.

choices.text: The first, since the second can be updated in an afternoon
choices.why: A three-year gap is rarely closed in an afternoon, and until then the drawing misleads.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson say a diagram worth keeping states on its face? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four questions.

choices.text: The question it answers
choices.why: Yes: a diagram drawn for a question can be judged against it.

choices.text: The date it describes
choices.why: Yes: a date tells the reader how far to trust it.

choices.text: The tool used to draw it
choices.why: The tool says nothing a reader needs; the date and the audience do.

choices.text: What it leaves out
choices.why: Yes: naming the omissions stops the reader filling them in.

prompt: How many services besides the monolith did Renata find connecting straight to the monolith's database?
hint: None of them was on the slide.

choices.text: Three
choices.why: Three is the number of services using the broker.

choices.text: Fourteen
choices.why: Fourteen is the count of all deployable services, the monolith among them.

choices.text: Five
choices.why: Right: five, Payments among them, and the slide showed none.

choices.text: Six
choices.why: Six is the number of services the slide drew, each with its own database.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a list of technologies says almost nothing about an architecture?
hint: PostgreSQL appears twice at Carreto, in two architectures.

choices.text: The same tools build opposite structures
choices.why: Right: one database per service and one shared by six both run on PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Technologies change too fast to be worth listing
choices.why: Pace of change is beside the point; even a stable list leaves elements and relations unsaid.

choices.text: Only open-source tools are architectural
choices.why: Licence is a criterion in lesson 5; it does not decide whether something is structure.

choices.text: Architects choose tools last, after deployment
choices.why: Tools come last in the chain of reasoning, not after the system is deployed.

prompt: A service publishes "please calculate a quote" to Kafka and fails if no reply arrives on another topic within two seconds. What is it, by the lesson?
hint: Who waits for whom?

choices.text: An event-driven design with loose coupling between the services
choices.why: The caller waits for a specific reply and fails without it, which is the opposite of loose coupling.

choices.text: A shared database by another name
choices.why: Nothing reads anyone else's tables; the messages travel through a broker.

choices.text: A synchronous chain wearing a broker's clothes
choices.why: Right: it inherits the synchronous version's weaknesses and adds the broker's moving parts.

choices.text: A log of facts
choices.why: A log of facts is read in each consumer's own time with nobody waiting on a reply.

prompt: Faced with the proposal to move Carreto to microservices, what does Renata do first?
hint: She does not say whether it is right.

choices.text: Rejects it, since Carreto is too small
choices.why: She does not rule on it at all; she asks for the problem first.

choices.text: Asks Platform to price a Kubernetes cluster for the twenty services
choices.why: Pricing a cluster accepts the technology before the problem is known.

choices.text: Asks those who would feel the problem what it is
choices.why: Right: deploy times, clashes over loads and waiting for reviews came back, and none was "no microservices".

choices.text: Approves a pilot with one service
choices.why: A pilot is still a solution chosen before the problem; she asks about the problem first.

prompt: About 3,000 trucks each send a position every 30 seconds. About how many positions per second reach Tracking?
hint: Trucks divided by the interval.

prompt: Put the steps of a sound technology choice in the lesson's order.
hint: The technology comes at the end of the chain.
items: State the quality attribute with a number
Choose the structural decision that delivers it
Pick the technology that implements that structure for this team
trap: Starting from the tool is the pattern behind "move to microservices because everyone does".

prompt: Which of these technology choices is architectural at Carreto, by lesson 1's test as this lesson applies it?
hint: How expensive is it to change your mind?

choices.text: The library Pricing uses to format dates
choices.why: Replacing it takes an afternoon inside one team.

choices.text: The logging format in the Driver app
choices.why: One team, one setting; cheap to reverse.

choices.text: A cloud's proprietary queue, called from forty places
choices.why: Right: leaving it means touching all forty, which makes the choice expensive to reverse.

choices.text: The text editor the engineers use
choices.why: Each engineer can switch tomorrow and the system would not notice.

prompt: What does the lesson name as the defence against résumé-driven choices?
hint: A question, asked every time.

choices.text: A list of approved technologies
choices.why: A list can help, but it does not ask what a proposal improves or costs.

choices.text: Which attribute improves, by how much, at what cost
choices.why: Right: a proposal that answers it is worth reading whatever it recommends.

choices.text: Suspicion of any tool that is less than five years old in production
choices.why: The lesson rejects suspicion of new tools as the defence.

choices.text: Letting the most senior engineer choose
choices.why: Seniority does not answer the question of what the change buys.

prompt: What is the main weakness of big design up front, by the lesson?
hint: When are the guesses discovered to be wrong?

choices.text: Paper designs are expensive to change
choices.why: Paper designs are cheap to change; that is the appeal of the approach.

choices.text: It fixes guesses that are corrected late, after code depends on them
choices.why: Right: most of what the design depends on is unknown, and the guesses are hardest to fix when they prove wrong.

choices.text: Teams waste work because they do not know where the project is going
choices.why: That is the problem big design up front tries to solve, not its weakness.

choices.text: Regulators forbid it
choices.why: No regulator is involved; the weakness is about information arriving late.

prompt: The Poppendiecks' name for the point at which failing to decide would eliminate an important alternative: the last ___ moment.
hint: Not the last possible one.

prompt: Bruno's Pix plan contains two decisions: whether payment requests carry a key the bank uses to refuse duplicates, and which client library talks to the bank. Which has its moment now?
hint: What does a mistake cost, and when does it arrive?

choices.text: The library, because it is the first line of code
choices.why: The library sits behind an interface and can be swapped in days; deciding now buys nothing.

choices.text: Both, so that the plan is complete before coding
choices.why: That is big design up front applied to a cheap decision as well as an expensive one.

choices.text: The duplicate key
choices.why: Right: a mistake arrives in money on the first day, and recovering a payment is slow.

choices.text: Neither, until the team has used the bank's sandbox for a month
choices.why: Waiting a month suits the library; the key would be decided by default in the first live payout.

prompt: Carreto's founders chose one Django application and one database in 2017. By the lesson, how should that decision be judged today?
hint: Six engineers then, fifty now.

choices.text: As a mistake that caused today's problems
choices.why: The founders were not wrong; the context moved under the decision.

choices.text: Right then; due for review now that the context moved
choices.why: Right: a decision made in a context is looked at again when the context changes, on purpose rather than by erosion.

choices.text: As still right, since it worked for years
choices.why: Working for years with six engineers says little about fifty in seven teams.

choices.text: As irrelevant, since decisions are not revisited
choices.why: The lesson argues the opposite: decisions are revisited when the context changes.

prompt: Why does the lesson say waiting is not free while a decision stays open?
hint: What do teams do around a gap?

choices.text: Open decisions block every team from working
choices.why: Teams keep working; the trouble is that they build around the gap.

choices.text: Information gets more expensive over time
choices.why: Information usually gets cheaper as a project learns; that is why waiting helps at first.

choices.text: Architects are measured by how many decisions they close
choices.why: No such measure appears; the cost is in the code built meanwhile.

choices.text: Work built around the gap is at risk of being undone
choices.why: Right: past its moment a deferred decision is taken by accident, by what the code already does.

prompt: Match each mistaken idea to the section of this lesson that answers it.
hint: Diagram, technology, phase.

pairs.left: "Our architecture is the slide in the onboarding deck"
pairs.right: a diagram is a view, not the architecture
a technology is not an architecture

pairs.left: "Architecture was done in the first quarter"

prompt: A proposal titled "Adopting GraphQL" spends one paragraph on the problem and six pages on the solution, considers no alternative, and promises a "modern, flexible API". What should Renata ask for first?
hint: Count the signs of a technology-first proposal.

choices.text: The problem, with numbers
choices.why: Right: the tool is in the title, the problem is short, there are no alternatives and the benefits are adjectives.

choices.text: A benchmark comparing GraphQL with REST
choices.why: A benchmark still compares solutions before anyone has stated what needs solving.

choices.text: A list of companies that use GraphQL in production
choices.why: That is the "Netflix did it" argument; other companies' problems are not Carreto's.

choices.text: A training plan for the teams
choices.why: Training answers a cost of the solution, which comes after knowing whether the solution fits.

prompt: A startup of four engineers writes a forty-page architecture document before its first customer. A year later the document is untouched and the code looks nothing like it. Which two ideas from this lesson explain what happened?
hint: One from the phase section, one from the diagram section.

choices.text: Résumé-driven development and erosion
choices.why: Nothing suggests tools were chosen for careers; the document was written too early and never revisited.

choices.text: Big design up front, then a plan read as a description
choices.why: Right: guesses fixed before the facts, then a stale document that people would believe.

choices.text: The last responsible moment and Conway's law
choices.why: They decided before the last responsible moment, which is the point; Conway's law is about team structure.

choices.text: No design at all, and drift
choices.why: They designed a great deal; the trouble was designing too much too early.
